content: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is defined as an abnormal enlargement of the infradiaphragmatic aorta, measuring either 30 mm or more in diameter or at least 50% larger than the expected normal diameter of the artery. This condition is uncommon in individuals under the age of 50, but its prevalence increases significantly with advancing age. Men are six times more likely to develop an AAA compared to women. Among individuals aged 65 to 80 years, the prevalence of AAA ranges from 1.3% in women to between 4% and 7.7% in men. The risk of aneurysm rupture escalates as the diameter of the aneurysm increases, particularly when it grows from 50 mm to 60 mm. Consequently, patients with an AAA measuring over 55 mm in diameter are typically referred for surgical repair, as the risk of rupture surpasses the risks associated with intervention. The traditional approach to AAA repair is open surgical repair (OSR), which involves a large abdominal incision and carries a significant risk of complications. However, two less invasive techniques have gained popularity in recent years: endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) and laparoscopic repair. EVAR involves the insertion of sheaths into the femoral artery in the groin, followed by the placement of a stent graft within the aneurysm sac under radiological guidance. This stent graft is anchored in place to create a new channel for blood flow. Laparoscopic repair, on the other hand, utilizes a laparoscope inserted through small abdominal incisions, and a synthetic graft is sewn into place to replace the weakened section of the aorta. Laparoscopic AAA repair can be further categorized into hand-assisted laparoscopic surgery (HALS), which involves an incision to allow the surgeon's hand to assist in the procedure, and total laparoscopic surgery (TLS), which is performed entirely laparoscopically. Both EVAR and laparoscopic repair are considered advantageous over OSR due to their minimally invasive nature. These techniques are associated with reduced pain, fewer complications, lower mortality rates, and shorter hospital stays. Current evidence suggests that elective laparoscopic AAA repair has a safety profile comparable to that of EVAR, with low rates of conversion to open surgery and similar mortality and morbidity rates. As a result, laparoscopic AAA repair may be a viable option for patients who are not suitable candidates for EVAR. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the perioperative mortality and operative time associated with laparoscopic (both total and hand-assisted) AAA repair compared to OSR or EVAR. Secondary objectives included assessing complication rates, all-cause mortality beyond 30 days, length of hospital and intensive care unit (ICU) stays, conversion and re-intervention rates, and quality of life outcomes. The Cochrane Vascular Information Specialist conducted a comprehensive search of relevant databases, including the Specialised Register and CENTRAL, as well as trial registries for ongoing or unpublished studies. Reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed for additional citations. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical trials comparing laparoscopic AAA repair (total or hand-assisted) with either OSR or EVAR. Only one RCT, involving 100 male participants, met the inclusion criteria. This trial compared hand-assisted laparoscopic repair with EVAR and reported outcomes such as in-hospital mortality, operative time, length of hospital stay, and lower limb ischemia. No in-hospital deaths were observed in the study. However, hand-assisted laparoscopic repair was associated with a longer operative time compared to EVAR, with a mean difference of 53 minutes (95% confidence interval [CI]: 36.49 to 69.51 minutes). The incidence of lower limb ischemia was similar between the two groups, with a risk ratio of 0.50 (95% CI: 0.05 to 5.34). The mean length of hospital stay was 4.2 days for the hand-assisted laparoscopic repair group and 3.4 days for the EVAR group. However, the standard deviations were not reported, making it impossible to independently assess the statistical significance of this difference. The quality of evidence was downgraded due to imprecision, as the review included only one small study with wide confidence intervals, and indirectness, as the study population consisted exclusively of male participants. No studies were identified that compared laparoscopic repair (total or hand-assisted) with OSR or total laparoscopic repair with EVAR. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness and safety of laparoscopic (total or hand-assisted) AAA repair compared to OSR or EVAR. High-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to provide more robust evidence on this topic.
